lines.text: Hello, I'm Joo, the sprite artist at Dallex. This is Sprite Studio.
It's my squared paper, on the one two eight K Spectrum.
Press two for the keys. Q, A, O and P move the cursor.
Press space to paint a square. Hold it and move to draw a line.
The pictures at the top show it at true size, as a player sees it.
And the numbers beside each row are that row's two bytes, in hex.
Press nought for the Lessons, from my drawing chapter.
Lesson one. A figure is just rows of dots.
Every square is one bit: inked is a one, empty is a zero.
Eight squares make a byte, so a row of sixteen is two bytes.
Read a byte from the left. Its squares are worth one hundred and twenty-eight,
then sixty-four, thirty-two, sixteen, eight, four, two and one.
On row one of the Mower, squares two and four are inked.
They're worth thirty-two and eight. Add them up, and you get forty.
In hex, forty is two sixteens and eight, so it's written two eight.
The right half of the row is empty, so that byte is zero zero.
Now I'll ink the very last square, worth one. Watch the right byte.
It reads zero one. You can read any sprite this way, a row at a time.
Lesson two. Tracing paper shows the last frame as little rings.
A moving figure is just a few pictures, shown one after another.
The Mower's two frames differ in only four rows, at its corners.
And the flip book plays both frames, at the speed the game uses.
Each picture stays up for four TV frames: nought point nought eight seconds.
Lesson four, the mask. It clears the scenery under the figure.
The Ring mask adds one dot all round the ink. F changes it.
The hatched squares are covered: the ink, the paper inside, and a ring.
Shape has no ring. Box covers the whole box.
Lesson three. The Test Ground puts it down three ways.
Copy wipes out the grass in its box. Mix lets the grass show through.
That's quick, but in busy grass the figure gets hard to see.
Mask then mix clears the grass under the mask, then adds the ink.
The figure stays solid, with the grass right up to its edge.
Lesson five. Why does drawing flicker?
The top copy rubs the figure out, then draws it again.
Watch it blink. For a moment there's only grass.
Draw once changes each dot just once, and never shows the gap.
So never rub out and redraw. Change each dot straight to its new value.
Lesson six. On the Spectrum, colour belongs to the cell.
The screen is cut into blocks, eight dots square.
Each block has one ink colour and one paper colour. Clashing blocks flash.
In Ink mode, every block the Mower touches takes its red ink.
But the grass in those blocks is ink too, so it turns red as well.
One dot off the grid, the Mower touches nine blocks instead of four.
That frame's wrong. Look. The grass round the Mower has turned red.
Press nine for the Sheet. It holds up to eight figures.
The data size counts the Row Codes a game would store.
A game often stores a figure eight times, shifted one dot further each time.
Shifting it right spills into the next byte, so each row needs three bytes.
Two frames, eight positions, sixteen rows, three bytes: seven hundred and sixty-eight.
Stored once, it's two frames, sixteen rows, two bytes: just sixty-four.
S saves the sheet to tape. X exports the figure, ready for a game.
Now draw something, flip it, and show me. I'll find your stray pixel.
